turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Quick question. When was the last time the whole stock market lost almost four percent in a single day?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Honestly, I'd have to think about it. That's the kind of day you remember.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Well, you're about to remember this one. Friday, the S and P five hundred fell three point seven percent, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped more than five percent.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And the wild part is that it happened right after the biggest initial public offering ever. Talk about bad timing.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Welcome to Nightly Brief, the show that takes the business news from your inbox and makes it make sense. I'm Maya.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And I'm Theo. It's Saturday, November twenty-first, and tonight's episode is built from one newsletter, Morning Brew's Saturday edition, which covers Friday's market action.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Here's what's on tonight's show. First, the big picture on interest rates and bonds. Then a quick look at deals, with one very famous lagoon. Then the companies, and there are some big names in the penalty box. After that, a tech industry segment, a walk through the markets scoreboard, and a wrap-up.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Grab a snack. Let's go.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Let's start with the thing under everything else, which is interest rates. The ten-year Treasury yield ended Friday at four point nine one two percent. That's down fourteen basis points on the day.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Okay, two terms to unpack. A Treasury is a bond, basically an I O U from the US government. You lend the government money, and it pays you interest. The yield is the return you get for holding that bond.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And a basis point?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: A basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point. So fourteen basis points is zero point one four of a percentage point. Finance people use the term so nobody gets confused between a rate moving by half a percent and half of a percentage point.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Got it. Now, here's the thing about yields. When a bond's price goes up, its yield goes down. They move in opposite directions, like a seesaw.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Right. So a fall in yield means investors were buying bonds, pushing the price up. The newsletter says that as money left tech stocks, it flowed into safer stuff, including government bonds.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: That's classic flight to safety. When stocks look scary, people park money somewhere boring and dependable. Boring is a compliment in a market crash.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And why should a regular person care about the ten-year yield? Because it's a benchmark. Mortgage rates, car loans and business borrowing costs tend to follow it. When it falls, borrowing gets a little cheaper, all else equal.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Now, rates also show up as a worry in tonight's tech story. The newsletter says investors fear that higher interest rates could temper borrowing by the big companies building artificial intelligence infrastructure.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Think about it like a house. If you're taking out a giant mortgage, the rate matters a lot. These companies are borrowing and spending at a giant scale to build data centers, so a higher rate makes that bill bigger.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: To give you context, the day before, the ten-year yield was at five point zero five two percent. So Friday's drop took it back under five percent.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Which is a nice round number to watch. Five percent on the ten-year is the kind of line commentators love to circle.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: On the economic calendar, we don't have a hard data release in tonight's newsletter. What the newsletter does flag is Monday, when options on Anthropic shares start trading.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: We'll explain options when we get to that story. Hold that thought.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Let me add a quick plain-English picture. Imagine the stock market as a crowded party and the bond market as the quiet kitchen where people go to catch their breath.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Friday, a lot of guests left the loud room. Some of them wandered into the kitchen, and that crowding is what pushed bond prices up and yields down.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And the Nasdaq, for anyone new, is a stock index heavy with technology companies. An index is just a scoreboard that tracks a basket of stocks, so you can see how a whole group is doing at once.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Which is why a tech-led day hits the Nasdaq hardest. When the big tech names fall, the scoreboard falls with them, and that's exactly what the Friday numbers show.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: For a regular person with a retirement account, the practical takeaway is that a day like this shows up in a statement, but the newsletter itself offers no prediction. It reports the facts, and the facts say fear is high.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Time for deals. And I promised you a lagoon. Iceland's Blue Lagoon, the famous geothermal spa that fills everyone's travel photos, went public on Friday.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Went public means it did an initial public offering, or I P O. That's when a private company sells shares to the public for the first time and lists on a stock exchange. Before an I P O, you can't just buy a piece of it. After, anyone with a brokerage account can.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: The Blue Lagoon trades on the Nasdaq Iceland exchange under the ticker B L U E. The offering raised about one hundred fifteen million dollars and valued the company at nearly one billion dollars.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Valued means the share price times all the shares. So the market is saying the whole business, which also runs hotels and a restaurant, is worth close to a billion.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Fun fact the newsletter drops. Tourism accounted for nine percent of Iceland's economy last year, according to Statistics Iceland.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Nine percent! So this is not a tiny niche. Though the newsletter also notes some people wonder how much room an already popular destination has left to grow.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: It's a funny contrast, because Blue Lagoon's debut came on the same day as the largest I P O story in the news, which is Anthropic. That one needs its own segment.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: It does. Let's go to Companies.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, held a record two trillion dollar I P O. Let me say that again. Two trillion dollars.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Wait, really? That's bigger than the economies of most countries.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: It's huge. And yet, the newsletter says the I P O couldn't reverse the unraveling of the so-called A I trade. On Friday Anthropic's shares fell eight point five percent, and at one point they nearly hit the I P O price of eighty-three dollars.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: That's an important idea. An I P O price is the price the first big buyers paid. If the shares drop back toward that level, it means the early excitement is nearly gone.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: The newsletter compares it to taking your high school sweetheart to a theme park restaurant and thinking it'll save the relationship. It didn't.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Rude, but fair.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Now, the bigger name in the rout is Nvidia, the chip maker. Its shares fell about fourteen percent on Friday, to one hundred twenty-five dollars and fifty-three cents.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And that's not a one-day story. Nvidia just posted its seventh weekly loss in a row, its longest losing streak since the two thousand eight financial crisis.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Why did it fall so hard on Friday? The newsletter says federal regulators announced they were probing Nvidia's accounting practices.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: An accounting probe means regulators are looking at how a company reports its financial numbers. Investors hate uncertainty, so even the start of a probe can hit the stock, before anyone knows if anything is wrong.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And that's layered on top of two other things. Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia in the wake of a scandal, and that was followed by tighter US chip export controls.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Export controls are rules about which products can be sold abroad. When they tighten, a chip company may lose customers in some countries.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Other chipmakers got hit too. AMD sank thirteen percent, Intel eight percent, and Broadcom twelve percent.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: So it wasn't one company's problem. It was the whole group.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And it spread beyond chips. Companies that spend piles of cash on data centers, like Alphabet, Meta and Amazon, also fell.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Those are the customers who buy the chips, so if investors worry they're spending too much, the whole chain gets nervous.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Okay, now a wildcard. An Anthropic mathematician, Levent Alpöge, claims he found a proof of the Riemann hypothesis while working with Claude.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: The Riemann hypothesis is a famous math puzzle about how prime numbers are spread out. Prime numbers are those like two, three, five and seven, which can only be divided evenly by one and themselves.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: It was first posed in eighteen fifty-nine, and it's one of the Millennium Prize Problems, a set of the hardest open questions in math.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Important caveat from the newsletter. It's a claim, and it only matters if the proof checks out. Mathematicians will have to verify it, and that takes time.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: But if it holds up, it'd be a major moment for A I in math.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And one lighter note from the entertainment side. The newsletter says Puck News reports that Disney has a new Home Alone movie in development, with Macaulay Culkin agreeing to play Kevin McCallister again.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: A tiny bit of holiday joy in a very red day.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: On to industry trends, and tonight it's mostly one industry. Technology and A I.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: First, the policy angle. President Trump said that the federal government would impose what he called a tremendous tax on US companies that build data centers in other countries.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: A data center is a giant warehouse of computers that powers things like cloud services and A I. Companies like Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon already have growing data center operations around the world.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: The newsletter says CNBC reported that the idea surprised the president's own staff when he brought it up at a press conference. The stated goal is to keep data centers in the US to help stay ahead of China on A I.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: There's also a domestic angle. Backlash to data centers has grown among the American public, and the newsletter says it helped some Democrats win in the midterm elections.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And that ties into investor fears. Analysts anticipate that newly elected Democrats, when they take office in January, may push regulation that would slow the data center buildout.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So we have three fears stacked up. Costly infrastructure spending, higher rates, and possible regulation.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Now, is there any good news? The newsletter offers two reads. First, institutional investors, meaning big funds, have been selling A I stocks in recent weeks. Analysts say that's consistent with the usual habit of taking profits before the end of the year.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Locking in gains, basically. If your portfolio is up a lot, you sell some to bank it before the calendar flips.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Second, a valuation point. Using data from a firm called FactSet, the price-to-expected-earnings ratio of tech companies is the lowest since twenty twenty.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Explain that one, Theo.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: A price-to-earnings ratio compares a stock's price with the profit per share a company is expected to earn. A lower number means you're paying less for each dollar of profit. So some analysts say tech is looking cheaper, since projected profits are still strong.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Cheaper doesn't mean it can't get cheaper still, though.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Exactly. And the rotation tells you where money went instead. The consumer staples sector, think groceries and household goods, rose zero point six eight percent on Friday.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Boring wins again.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And this brings us back to Monday, when options on Anthropic shares start trading. An option is a contract that gives you the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell a stock at a set price by a set date.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: The newsletter says that will give a clearer sense of how much appetite retail investors have for the shares.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Retail investors are everyday people like you and me, as opposed to big institutions. So Monday is a real test.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Let's do the scoreboard. These are Friday's closing numbers from Morning Brew, with Bitcoin as of five thirty p m Eastern.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: The S and P five hundred closed at six thousand nine hundred ten, down three point seven percent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average finished at forty-eight thousand one hundred forty-seven, down one point nine percent.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And the Nasdaq closed at twenty-two thousand six hundred eighteen, down five point three percent.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: The newsletter's own text says the Nasdaq dropped five point six percent, while its data table says five point three. We're going with the table, and we're flagging the difference.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: There's another mismatch. The newsletter says the market looked like a correction, and also says the S and P entered bear market territory.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Those are different things. A correction is usually a drop of ten percent or more from a recent high. A bear market is twenty percent or more. We can't confirm which one it is from this newsletter, so treat that as unresolved.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Next, the ten-year Treasury yield, four point nine one two percent, down fourteen basis points, as we discussed.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And Bitcoin sat at about fifty-eight thousand nine hundred twenty-three dollars, down five point one percent. Nvidia, as we said, closed at one hundred twenty-five dollars fifty-three cents.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: What about oil and gold, which are on our usual scoreboard?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Tonight's newsletter doesn't list levels for those, so we're leaving them out rather than guessing. Same for the comparison against six months and a year ago. Our data sources weren't reachable tonight, so those are marked not available in the email.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Honest answers beat made-up numbers.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Okay, three-point recap. Theo, take it away.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: One. Tech got crushed on Friday. Nvidia, the other chipmakers and the big spenders on data centers all fell, and the Nasdaq gave back all its gains for the year.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Two. Money moved to safety. The ten-year yield dropped fourteen basis points to four point nine one two percent, and consumer staples rose.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Three. Even a record Anthropic I P O couldn't stop the slide. Fears about spending, rates and regulation are all in the mix, though some analysts say valuations now look lower.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: What to watch next? Monday, when options on Anthropic start trading, and whether the selling in chip stocks continues.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And keep an eye on the Nvidia accounting probe, since any new details could move the whole sector.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: That's Nightly Brief for Saturday. I'm Maya.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And I'm Theo. This is news, not investment advice. Have a great weekend, and we'll see you tomorrow.
